questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The most common position of the appendix is:
questions.exp: The retrocaecal position is the commonest site of the appendix, accounting for about 74% of cases. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The least common appendiceal position is:
questions.exp: Postileal appendix is the least common position listed on the page, around 0.5%. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: Which appendiceal position is present in about 21% of patients?
questions.exp: Pelvic appendix is shown as the second commonest position, approximately 21%. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: Which appendiceal position is approximately 1%?
questions.exp: Preileal appendix is labelled as about 1% in the position diagram. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: Which of the following correctly matches the less common positions of the appendix with their frequencies?
questions.exp: The diagram labels paracaecal appendix as about 2% and subcaecal appendix as about 0.5%. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The appendicular base is identified intraoperatively at the:
opts: Junction of the three taeniae coli
questions.exp: The base of the appendix is constant in position and lies at the junction of the three taeniae coli. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: McBurney's point corresponds to the:
opts: Base of appendix and point of maximum tenderness
Tip of appendix and point of rebound
questions.exp: McBurney's point marks the base of the appendix and is the site of maximum tenderness in appendicitis. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The appendicular artery usually arises from the:
opts: Lower division of the ileocolic artery
questions.exp: The appendicular artery is a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: A surgically important feature of the appendicular artery is that it is a:
opts: Branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
Terminal branch of the middle colic artery
questions.exp: The appendicular artery is an end artery, which is why thrombosis can readily precipitate ischemia. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: Deficient blood supply close to the tip of appendix predisposes to:
questions.exp: The page specifically notes deficient supply near the tip as the site of thrombosis and perforation. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The accessory appendicular artery is also called the:
questions.exp: The accessory appendicular artery is named the artery of Seshachalam. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: The accessory appendicular artery most commonly arises from the:
questions.exp: The accessory appendicular artery is described as a branch of the posterior caecal artery. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: At birth, the appendix is characteristically:
opts: Short and broad at its junction with the caecum
Long and narrow with a fixed retrocaecal position
questions.exp: Developmentally, the appendix is short and broad at its junction with the caecum at birth. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: By about what age does the appendix become tubular in structure?
questions.exp: The developmental note on the page states that by 2 years the appendix becomes a tubular structure. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
questions.q: Growth of the caecum leads to rotation of the appendix into a predominantly __________ position.
questions.exp: With growth of the caecum, the appendix rotates into a retrocaecal, intraperitoneal position. (Book p208)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The most common type of acute appendicitis is:
questions.exp: The chapter classifies obstructive appendicitis as the most common type. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The most common obstructing factor in acute appendicitis is:
questions.exp: Luminal obstruction by a fecolith is listed as the most common cause of obstructive appendicitis. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: All of the following may obstruct the appendiceal lumen EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The page lists fecolith, food particle, roundworm/ascariasis, foreign body and carcinoid tumour as obstructive causes; portal pyaemia is a complication, not a cause. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Catarrhal non-obstructive appendicitis is particularly described in:
questions.exp: The non-obstructive catarrhal type is noted on the page as occurring in children. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Approximately what proportion of acute appendicitis is non-obstructive (catarrhal)?
questions.exp: The chapter gives non-obstructive catarrhal appendicitis a frequency of about 10-15%. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Acute appendicitis is relatively uncommon in:
questions.exp: The incidence section specifically notes that appendicitis is uncommon in infants and the elderly. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Peak incidence of acute appendicitis is in:
questions.exp: Acute appendicitis peaks in the teenage years and early twenties. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Regarding sex distribution of acute appendicitis, the chapter states:
opts: Males are affected more often than females
Females are affected more often than males
questions.exp: The incidence note states males are affected more commonly than females. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The most common symptom of acute appendicitis is:
questions.exp: Pain is listed as the most common symptom of acute appendicitis. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Classically, appendicular pain begins in the __________ and later shifts to the __________.
questions.exp: The classical sequence is visceral periumbilical pain followed by migration to the right iliac fossa where it becomes parietal pain. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The early periumbilical pain of acute appendicitis is best described as:
questions.exp: Early appendicular pain is visceral and therefore felt around the umbilicus. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: When pain in appendicitis localizes to the right iliac fossa, it reflects:
questions.exp: Once the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed, the pain shifts to the right iliac fossa and becomes localized. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Murphy's triad in acute appendicitis consists of pain, fever and:
questions.exp: The triangular diagram on the page places pain, fever, and nausea with vomiting together as Murphy's triad. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Which symptom is listed separately in addition to Murphy's triad in acute appendicitis?
questions.exp: Anorexia is listed as another common symptom alongside the classical triad. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: A patient who points precisely to McBurney's point as the site of maximum tenderness is demonstrating:
questions.exp: Pointing sign refers to indicating McBurney's point as the site of maximal tenderness. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: Rovsing sign is considered positive when:
opts: Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa
Extension of the hip causes right iliac fossa pain
Internal rotation of the hip causes pelvic pain
questions.exp: Rovsing sign is positive when pressing the left iliac fossa produces pain in the right iliac fossa. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: One mechanism proposed for Rovsing sign is:
opts: Displacement of bowel and air toward the right, irritating the appendix
Stretch of the ureter by hip extension
questions.exp: The page explains Rovsing sign by displacement of bowel and air to the right, thereby irritating the appendix. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The Cope psoas test may be elicited by all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Forced internal rotation of the right hip
Flexion of the right hip against resistance
questions.exp: Psoas sign is elicited by flexion of the right hip against resistance or by hyperextension of the right hip; internal rotation belongs to the obturator test. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
questions.q: The obturator sign in appendicitis is produced by pain during:
opts: Flexion and internal rotation of the right hip
questions.exp: The page defines the obturator sign as pain caused by flexion and internal rotation of the right hip. (Book p209)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Dunphy sign refers to:
opts: Pain in epigastrium on pressing RIF
Pain on pulling the right testis
questions.exp: Dunphy sign is pain in the right lower abdomen precipitated by coughing. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Aaron sign in appendicitis is:
opts: Epigastric pain on pressing the right iliac fossa
questions.exp: Aaron sign is described as pain felt in the epigastrium when the right iliac fossa is pressed. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Tenhorn sign is positive when:
opts: Pulling the right testis causes right iliac fossa pain
The left iliac fossa is pressed
The right hip is internally rotated
questions.exp: Tenhorn sign is pain in the right iliac fossa produced by pulling the right testis. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: In retrocaecal appendicitis, abdominal rigidity is typically:
questions.exp: Retrocaecal appendicitis may lack the usual anterior peritoneal irritation, so abdominal rigidity can be absent. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Which sign is especially associated with retrocaecal appendicitis?
questions.exp: Retrocaecal appendicitis characteristically gives a positive psoas sign. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Pelvic appendicitis commonly causes increased frequency of micturition because of:
questions.exp: A pelvic appendix irritates the bladder, leading to urinary frequency. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Rectal irritation by a pelvic appendix may produce:
opts: Pelvic diarrhoea and pain on DRE
questions.exp: Pelvic appendicitis may irritate the rectum, causing pelvic diarrhoea and pain on digital rectal examination. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Which form of appendicitis is described as the most difficult to diagnose because signs may be absent?
questions.exp: The chapter specifically states that postileal appendicitis is the most difficult to diagnose because of paucity of signs. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: A clue to postileal appendicitis on examination may be:
questions.exp: Postileal appendicitis may show little beyond slight pain on deep pressure. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: A typical laboratory profile in acute appendicitis includes:
opts: Raised TLC, neutrophilia with left shift, and raised CRP
questions.exp: The investigation section lists raised total leukocyte count, neutrophilia with left shift, and elevated CRP. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: The preferred imaging test according to age group is correctly matched in:
questions.exp: The page advises ultrasound for children and contrast-enhanced CT for adults. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: In pregnant women with suspected appendicitis, the imaging options suggested are:
questions.exp: For pregnancy, the imaging section specifically mentions USG/MRI. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Which ultrasound finding best supports acute appendicitis?
questions.exp: A blind-ending tubular structure is the classic ultrasonographic appearance of an inflamed appendix. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as an ultrasonographic feature of appendicitis on the page?
questions.exp: The page lists blind-ending tubular structure, probe tenderness, periappendiceal fluid, and appendicolith/fecolith; portal venous gas is not listed. (Book p210)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: In the Alvarado score, migration of pain to the right lower quadrant scores:
questions.exp: Migration of pain to the right lower quadrant carries 1 point in the Alvarado score. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Tenderness in the right lower quadrant contributes how many Alvarado points?
questions.exp: Right lower quadrant tenderness is one of the heavier-weighted criteria and scores 2 points. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Leukocytosis in the Alvarado score is worth:
questions.exp: Leukocytosis contributes 2 points in the Alvarado system. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Shift of white blood cells to the left in the Alvarado score is worth:
questions.exp: A left shift contributes 1 point in the original Alvarado score. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a 1-point item in the Alvarado score?
questions.exp: Migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, rebound pain, fever, and left shift each score 1; leukocytosis scores 2. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: What is the maximum total Alvarado score shown in the chapter?
questions.exp: The table totals the Alvarado score to a maximum of 10. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: An Alvarado score below 5 is interpreted as:
questions.exp: The interpretation table classifies a score below 5 as unlikely appendicitis. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: An Alvarado score of 5-8 suggests that appendicitis should be:
questions.exp: The table advises that a score of 5-8 should be confirmed with ultrasound. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: An Alvarado score of 9-10 makes acute appendicitis:
questions.exp: A score of 9-10 is interpreted as highly likely appendicitis. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: The Alvarado score is particularly useful because it has a high:
questions.exp: The page explicitly notes the score has a high negative predictive value. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: The modified Alvarado score differs from the original because it does NOT include:
opts: Shift of white blood cells to the left
questions.exp: The modified Alvarado score omits the left shift component. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: A child with right iliac fossa pain, high fever and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes most likely has:
questions.exp: The differential section highlights Yersinia mesenteric adenitis in children, especially when fever is high and nodes are enlarged. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: A common differential diagnosis of appendicitis in infants and children is:
questions.exp: Among children, the page lists intussusception as an important differential diagnosis. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: An adult woman with cyclical mid-cycle pain mimicking appendicitis is likely experiencing:
questions.exp: Mittelschmerz is specifically described as mid-cycle ovulatory pain in adult females. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Which of the following is an adult/elderly differential diagnosis for appendicitis according to the page?
questions.exp: For adults and the elderly, the chapter lists ureteric colic among the common differentials. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: Conservative management of appendicitis includes all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The conservative plan is NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics with aerobic and anaerobic cover, and painkillers; laxatives/high-fibre diet are not part of this page's regimen. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: When nonoperative management is used for appendicitis, antibiotic coverage should include:
questions.exp: The chapter specifically advises IV antibiotics covering both aerobic and anaerobic organisms. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: The anaerobic organism specifically mentioned in the conservative antibiotic plan for appendicitis is:
questions.exp: Bacteroides is named as the anaerobic target in conservative therapy. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
questions.q: A major disadvantage of conservative management in appendicitis is:
questions.exp: The page points out the main drawback of conservative treatment is a high recurrence rate. (Book p211)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The gridiron incision used for open appendicectomy is a:
questions.exp: The page identifies the gridiron incision as a muscle-splitting incision. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Rutherford Morrison's incision is described as a:
questions.exp: Rutherford Morrison's incision is specifically labeled muscle cutting. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Which muscles are cut in Rutherford Morrison's incision?
opts: External oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.exp: The page lists external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis under the muscle-cutting incision. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Lanz incision is also known as the:
questions.exp: Lanz incision is described as the skin crease or bikini incision. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The Lanz incision is placed approximately:
opts: At the tip of the 12th rib
At the midline above the umbilicus
questions.exp: The page notes the Lanz incision as lying about 2 cm below the umbilicus. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: In appendicular perforation, the incision specifically mentioned is:
questions.exp: The lower midline abdominal incision is mentioned as being used in appendicular perforation. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Which structure is encountered immediately after skin during open appendicectomy?
questions.exp: The listed order starts with skin followed by superficial fascia. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The superficial fascia encountered in appendicectomy consists of:
questions.exp: The page explicitly labels superficial fascia as Camper's and Scarpa's. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: How many ports are shown for laparoscopic appendicectomy?
questions.exp: The laparoscopic diagram on the page shows a three-port technique. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: A standard laparoscopic appendicectomy port setup includes all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The chapter shows infraumbilical, left iliac fossa and suprapubic ports; a right hypochondrial port is not listed. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The larger laparoscopic port shown for appendicectomy is the:
questions.exp: The port diagram labels the infraumbilical port as 12 mm, with the others as 5 mm. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The first operative step in appendicectomy is to locate the appendix by finding the:
opts: Junction of the three taeniae coli
questions.exp: Whether open or laparoscopic, the appendix is first identified at the convergence of the three taeniae coli. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: After identifying the appendix, the next essential step is to:
opts: Ligate the appendicular artery and bare the appendix
questions.exp: The stepwise sequence on the page is to ligate the appendicular artery and bare the appendix. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: To reduce the risk of stump appendicitis, the appendiceal stump should usually be kept:
questions.exp: The operative illustration specifically recommends a stump length below 4-5 mm. (Book p212)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If the appendix cannot be found during surgery, the surgeon should:
opts: Locate the taeniae coli and follow them to their junction
questions.exp: When the appendix is not obvious, following the taeniae coli to their junction leads to the appendicular base. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If the appendix appears normal at operation, the surgeon should inspect the:
opts: Last 2 feet of ileum for Meckel's diverticulum
questions.exp: The chapter advises checking the last 2 feet of ileum for Meckel's diverticulum if the appendix is not inflamed. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum is found while the appendix is normal, the recommended treatment is:
questions.exp: The Meckel's algorithm on the page shows inflamed Meckel's diverticulum should be resected and anastomosed. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If Meckel's diverticulum is not inflamed when the appendix is being explored, the page advises:
questions.exp: The flowchart states that if Meckel's is not inflamed, appendicectomy is done. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: In an inflamed appendiceal base, which intraoperative maneuver should be avoided?
opts: Using a linear stapler when caecal base is healthy
questions.exp: The page clearly says not to crush an inflamed appendiceal base. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If the appendiceal base is inflamed, the stump is commonly dealt with by:
opts: Burying it with a purse-string suture or Z-stitch
Exteriorizing the caecum as a stoma
questions.exp: The chapter specifically recommends burying the inflamed base with a purse-string or Z stitch. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: A linear stapler may be used for an inflamed appendiceal base when the:
questions.exp: The page notes that a linear stapler is appropriate if the caecal base remains healthy. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: If the appendiceal base and adjacent caecal wall are gangrenous, the operation of choice is:
questions.exp: Gangrene involving the appendiceal base and adjoining caecal wall requires right hemicolectomy. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: In appendicitis associated with Crohn's disease, appendicectomy is safest when the caecum is:
questions.exp: The Crohn's algorithm says appendicectomy is done when the caecum is healthy, lowering fistula risk. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: When the caecum is inflamed in Crohn's disease with appendicitis, the preferred approach is:
questions.exp: If the caecum is inflamed in Crohn's disease, the page recommends conservative management because appendicectomy raises fistula risk. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The most common postoperative complication after appendicectomy is:
questions.exp: Wound infection is marked as the most common complication following appendicectomy. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Injury to the right iliohypogastric nerve during appendicectomy predisposes to:
questions.exp: The page links right iliohypogastric nerve injury with later risk of right inguinal hernia. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Fever with pelvic diarrhoea after appendicectomy should raise suspicion of:
questions.exp: Pelvic abscess is specifically described as presenting with fever and pelvic diarrhoea. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The investigation of choice for suspected postoperative pelvic abscess is:
questions.exp: The note under pelvic abscess specifies CECT as the investigation. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Stump appendicitis is more likely when the appendiceal stump measures:
questions.exp: A residual stump longer than 4-5 mm raises the risk of stump appendicitis. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Appendicectomy performed as an emergency procedure is classified as a:
questions.exp: The wound classification note on the page labels emergency appendicectomy as contaminated. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Elective appendicectomy is classified as a:
questions.exp: The note classifies elective appendicectomy as clean-contaminated. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: The 'policeman of the abdomen' in appendicular inflammation is the:
questions.exp: The page calls the greater omentum the policeman of the abdomen because it walls off inflamed appendix. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Which factor predisposes children to appendicular perforation?
questions.exp: Children perforate early because the protective greater omentum is underdeveloped. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Appendicular perforation in the elderly is favoured by:
opts: Atherosclerosis of the walls of the greater omentum
questions.exp: In the elderly, atherosclerosis in the omental vessels weakens this protective barrier and promotes perforation. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a risk factor for quick appendicular perforation?
questions.exp: The page states that presence of an appendicolith leads to quick perforation. (Book p213)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Generalized peritonitis due to appendicular perforation classically shows all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The page lists rebound tenderness, guarding, and rigidity as features of peritonitis; shifting dullness is not part of that list. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The recommended incision for appendicitis presenting with diffuse peritonitis is:
questions.exp: For appendicitis with peritonitis, the chapter recommends appendicectomy by lower midline incision. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Appendicitis is the most common __________ abdominal emergency in pregnancy.
questions.exp: The chapter explicitly labels appendicitis as the most common non-obstetric abdominal emergency in pregnancy. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Pain of appendicitis in pregnancy is most commonly felt in the:
questions.exp: Even in pregnancy, most patients still present with pain in the right iliac fossa, though in some it may be slightly higher. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: If ultrasound is inconclusive in pregnant appendicitis, the next imaging study suggested is:
questions.exp: The imaging algorithm for pregnancy advises MRI when ultrasound is inconclusive. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Delayed diagnosis or perforation of appendicitis in pregnancy increases the risk of:
questions.exp: The significance note directly links untreated/perforated appendicitis in pregnancy with fetal loss and preterm labour. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: According to the chapter, laparoscopic appendicectomy in pregnancy is:
opts: Restricted to the second trimester only
questions.exp: The treatment line explicitly says laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done in all trimesters. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: In the comparison note on pregnancy-related abdominal emergencies, cholecystitis is managed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the:
questions.exp: The chapter contrasts appendicitis with cholecystitis and notes laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the second trimester. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: In the pregnancy algorithm, diffuse peritonitis mandates:
questions.exp: The management flowchart directs that diffuse peritonitis in pregnancy should be resuscitated and operated upon. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: An appendicular lump is best described as:
opts: A jumbled mass of omentum and bowel over the inflamed appendix
questions.exp: The page defines appendicular lump as omentum and bowel matted over the inflamed appendix. (Book p214)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: A classical clinical clue to appendicular lump is:
opts: Previous acute right iliac fossa pain with a palpable RIF mass
Mass in the left iliac fossa after constipation
questions.exp: The page describes appendicular lump by a history of acute RIF pain and a right iliac fossa mass on examination. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Ochsner-Sherren regimen is essentially:
questions.exp: Ochsner-Sherren regimen is the classical expectant non-operative treatment for appendicular lump. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which parameter is monitored during Ochsner-Sherren treatment of appendicular lump?
questions.exp: The monitoring list includes vitals, temperature, pain, and the size of the lump. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which of the following indicates recovery during conservative management of appendicular lump?
opts: Fall in pulse rate, fever, lump size and TLC
Rise in pulse rate and fever
questions.exp: Recovery is marked by decreased pulse, lower fever, shrinking lump, and falling TLC. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: After recovery from an appendicular lump, interval appendicectomy is advised after:
questions.exp: The page recommends interval appendicectomy 6 weeks after recovery from appendicular lump. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: During conservative treatment of appendicular lump, worsening with chills, rising TLC and increasing lump size suggests:
questions.exp: A worsening course with fever, chills, larger lump, and rising TLC indicates appendicular abscess formation. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The preferred drainage route for appendicular abscess in the chapter is:
questions.exp: Appendicular abscess is managed by extraperitoneal drainage, often with a pigtail catheter. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The most common appendicular tumour is:
questions.exp: The page states that the most common appendicular tumour is neuroendocrine tumour/carcinoid tumour. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The appendix is the most common site for which tumour mentioned in the chapter?
questions.exp: Under appendicular tumour, the page specifically notes the appendix as the most common site for NET/carcinoid. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Most appendiceal neuroendocrine tumours arise at the:
questions.exp: The chapter labels the tip as the site of about 70% of appendiceal NETs. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The usual age group for appendiceal neuroendocrine tumour is:
questions.exp: Appendiceal NET is shown as a tumour of 40-50 years in this chapter. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Diagnosis of appendiceal NET is often:
questions.exp: The page states that appendiceal NET is often diagnosed incidentally. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Immunohistochemical markers used for appendiceal NET include:
questions.exp: Synaptophysin and chromogranin A are the IHC stains listed for appendiceal NET. (Book p215)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: An appendiceal NET larger than 2 cm or close to the base is managed by:
questions.exp: The treatment flowchart directs right hemicolectomy for tumours more than 2 cm or close to the base. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: A small appendiceal NET under 1 cm and away from the base is treated with:
opts: Simple appendicectomy with removal of mesoappendix
questions.exp: For NET less than 1 cm and away from the base, the chart advises simple appendicectomy and removal of mesoappendix. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: A 1-2 cm appendiceal NET warrants right hemicolectomy in the chapter when it is:
questions.exp: The page specifically escalates 1-2 cm appendiceal NETs to right hemicolectomy when they are poorly differentiated or stage T4. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The most important prognostic factor in appendiceal NET is:
questions.exp: The page clearly states that size is the most important prognostic factor. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Tumour grade in appendiceal NET is determined by:
questions.exp: Grade is determined by mitotic index and Ki-67 according to the chapter. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Goblet cell carcinoma of appendix is best described as:
opts: A rare tumour with both neuroendocrine and glandular differentiation
questions.exp: Goblet cell carcinoma is rare, not a true NET, and shows both neuroendocrine and glandular differentiation. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Compared with ordinary appendiceal NET, goblet cell carcinoma has greater tendency for:
questions.exp: The page notes higher propensity for nodal and peritoneal dissemination in goblet cell carcinoma than in NET. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Goblet cell carcinoma of the appendix is treated as:
opts: Adenocarcinoma with right radical hemicolectomy plus chemotherapy
questions.exp: Management is the same as adenocarcinoma: right radical hemicolectomy with chemotherapy. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Disseminated peritoneal adenomucinosis (DPAM) is characterized in the chapter as:
questions.exp: DPAM is specifically described as locally invasive and slow growing. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Peritoneal mucinous carcinomatosis (PMCA) differs from DPAM because it is:
opts: More aggressive and associated with distant metastasis
questions.exp: The page contrasts PMCA with DPAM by noting PMCA is more aggressive and shows distant metastasis. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which resection status means microscopic freedom from disease?
questions.exp: R0 resection means no microscopic residual disease remains. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which resection status indicates microscopic disease is left behind?
questions.exp: R1 means disease persists microscopically after resection. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which resection status indicates gross disease is left behind?
questions.exp: R2 resection means macroscopic or gross disease remains. (Book p216)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Pseudomyxoma peritonei refers to:
opts: Peritoneal cavity filled with mucin-like material
questions.exp: The chapter defines pseudomyxoma peritonei as the peritoneal cavity being filled with mucin-like substance. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The commonest source of pseudomyxoma peritonei mentioned in this appendix chapter is:
questions.exp: The causes listed for pseudomyxoma peritonei include appendiceal mucinous neoplasms, ovarian mucinous neoplasms, and primary peritoneal cancer. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Progressive abdominal distention with bowel obstruction in a patient with appendiceal mucinous neoplasm suggests:
questions.exp: The clinical features of pseudomyxoma peritonei on this page are progressive abdominal distention and bowel obstruction. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: The CT finding specifically mentioned in pseudomyxoma peritonei is:
questions.exp: Investigation by CECT demonstrates mucin deposits in the omentum. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: A tissue diagnosis in pseudomyxoma peritonei can be obtained by:
questions.exp: The investigation list includes omental biopsy for diagnosis. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Cytoreductive surgery for pseudomyxoma peritonei may include all EXCEPT:
opts: Splenectomy as mandatory in every patient
Stripping of peritoneum and removal of mucin
questions.exp: The page lists appendicectomy, right hemicolectomy when appendix is primarily involved, omentectomy, peritoneal stripping, and in females TAH with BSO; routine mandatory splenectomy is not listed. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: If the appendix is the primary site involved in pseudomyxoma peritonei, the colorectal resection advised is:
questions.exp: Primary appendiceal involvement is treated with right hemicolectomy in the cytoreductive plan. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: In women undergoing cytoreduction for pseudomyxoma peritonei, the gynecologic procedure mentioned is:
questions.exp: The page specifically includes total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in females. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: HIPEC in pseudomyxoma peritonei uses chemotherapy heated to approximately:
questions.exp: The HIPEC note specifies heated chemotherapy at about 40-41°C. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: Which drugs are listed for HIPEC in this chapter?
questions.exp: The HIPEC regimen listed on the page uses mitomycin-C and paclitaxel. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: After instillation during HIPEC, the chemotherapy is drained after:
questions.exp: The chapter states the heated chemotherapy is drained after 30 minutes. (Book p217)

questions.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
questions.q: A stated advantage of HIPEC is:
opts: Improved local control and enhanced efficacy of chemotherapy
questions.exp: The page notes HIPEC is advised for local control and to improve the efficacy of chemotherapy. (Book p217)

units.title: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development
units.sec: Appendix: Anatomy, Position, Blood Supply and Development · p208
units.guide: Start with fixed anatomy. Retrocaecal is the common position, postileal the rare one, and the appendicular base is the dependable landmark at the meeting point of the three taeniae coli. The artery is an end artery running in the mesoappendix, so tip ischemia and perforation matter; remember also the accessory artery of Seshachalam and the developmental shift toward a retrocaecal intraperitoneal appendix.

units.title: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features
units.sec: Acute Appendicitis: Types, Causes, Incidence and Classical Clinical Features · p209
units.guide: Acute appendicitis is usually obstructive and most often blocked by a fecolith, peaking in teenage and early adult males. Clinically the story is classic: visceral periumbilical pain migrates to the right iliac fossa, bringing Murphy's triad, anorexia, McBurney tenderness and the bedside signs every exam expects.

units.title: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations
units.sec: Appendicitis: Location-specific Signs and Investigations · p210
units.guide: Next come the subtleties - Dunphy, Aaron and Tenhorn - and then the location-specific clues. Retrocaecal appendicitis may hide rigidity, pelvic appendicitis irritates bladder and rectum, and postileal disease can be the most elusive. Support the diagnosis with leukocytosis, left shift, CRP, age-appropriate imaging, and ultrasound findings such as a blind-ending tubular structure or appendicolith.

units.title: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management
units.sec: Alvarado Score, Differential Diagnosis and Conservative Management · p211
units.guide: The Alvarado table must be usable, not merely memorized: tenderness and leukocytosis weigh 2 points each, the rest score 1, and the whole system totals 10 with a strong negative predictive value. The modified score drops the left shift. Finish the page by separating pediatric mimics, adult causes, female gynecologic mimics, and when conservative treatment is chosen, its elements and limitation - recurrence.

units.title: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications
units.sec: Appendicectomy: Incisions, Laparoscopy, Intraoperative Scenarios and Postoperative Complications · p212
units.guide: Open appendicectomy lives in its incisions: gridiron splits muscle, Rutherford Morrison cuts it, Lanz is the bikini incision, and perforation may need a lower midline approach. Laparoscopy uses three ports and a short stump. Intraoperatively, follow taeniae coli if lost, check the distal ileum when the appendix is normal, respect an inflamed base, and know the complications - especially wound infection, pelvic abscess and stump appendicitis.

units.title: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours
units.sec: Appendicular Peritonitis, Pregnancy, Appendicular Lump and Appendicular Tumours · p214
units.guide: This final run through the chapter covers the dangerous variants and the tumors. Peritonitis and pregnancy change incision choice, imaging, and urgency; appendicular lump demands disciplined Ochsner-Sherren monitoring and delayed surgery unless it suppurates. Then switch gears to appendiceal tumours: NET by size and base, goblet cell carcinoma as adenocarcinoma, and finally pseudomyxoma peritonei with cytoreduction and HIPEC.
